about: The scripted AI lesson for p4-radioactivity (2026-11-27, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p4-nuclear-model.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about the radiation that comes out of the centre of some atoms: what it is, what stops it, and where it comes from.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. What is in the nucleus of an atom?
steps.right: Yes: protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside it.

wrong.electrons: Not quite: electrons are outside the nucleus. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons.
wrong.only: Not quite: electrons are outside the nucleus. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons.

idk.hint: Electrons are outside the nucleus. Which two particles are left?

steps.answerWhy: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons are outside it.

steps.question: Second: what does the atomic number of an atom count?
steps.right: Yes: the atomic number counts the protons, and it decides the element.

wrong.both: Not quite: that is the mass number. The atomic number counts the protons only.
wrong.neutrons: Not quite: the atomic number counts the protons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

idk.hint: The atomic number decides the element. Is that set by the protons or the neutrons?

steps.answerWhy: The atomic number is the number of protons, which decides the element.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Some nuclei are unstable: they cannot stay as they are forever.
Radiation is energy or particles given out by something. A fire gives out heat and light. Here it means what comes out of a nucleus.
An unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. This is called radioactive decay.
Radioactive decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, or when. It is like rolling dice.
The activity of a source is the number of its nuclei that decay each second. It is measured in becquerels (Bq): 1 Bq is one decay each second.
A Geiger-Muller tube is a detector that clicks for each bit of radiation that reaches it. The count rate is the number it records each second.

steps.question: A source has an activity of 300 Bq. What does that mean?

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 nuclei decay each second.
wrong.number: Not quite: activity is not how many nuclei there are. It is how many decay each second: 300.
wrong.time: Not quite: activity is a rate, not a time. 300 Bq means 300 nuclei decay each second.

idk.hint: 1 Bq is one decay each second. So what is 300 Bq?

steps.answerWhy: An activity of 300 Bq means 300 nuclei decay each second.

steps.text: The radiation from a nucleus comes in a few kinds. This lesson takes three of them in turn, starting with alpha.
An alpha particle (α) is 2 protons and 2 neutrons stuck together: the same as the nucleus of a helium atom.
When a nucleus gives out an alpha particle, it loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Its mass number falls by 4 and its atomic number falls by 2. It becomes a different element.

steps.question: A nucleus with mass number 226 gives out an alpha particle. What is the mass number of the new nucleus?
steps.right: Yes: 222. It loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so 226 − 4 = 222.

wrong.other: Not quite: 222. The mass number falls by 4: 226 − 4 = 222.
wrong.two: Not quite: 222. An alpha particle holds 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so the mass number falls by 4: 226 − 4 = 222.
wrong.add: Not quite: 222. The nucleus loses the alpha particle, so take 4 away: 226 − 4 = 222.

idk.hint: An alpha particle holds 4 particles: 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Take them away from 226.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle has a mass number of 4, so the new mass number is 226 − 4 = 222.

steps.text: Radiation that knocks electrons off atoms as it passes is called ionising radiation. An atom that loses electrons becomes an ion.
Alpha is highly ionising: each alpha particle makes lots of ions. That uses up its energy fast, so it only travels about 5 cm in air, and a sheet of paper stops it.
Outside the body, alpha is stopped by the skin. Breathed in or swallowed, alpha is very dangerous, because it ionises so much inside the body.

steps.question: Why is a source that gives out alpha most dangerous when it is swallowed?

options.text: Alpha ionises a lot, and inside the body nothing shields you
Alpha travels a long way through the body
Alpha cannot be stopped by anything

steps.right: Yes: skin stops it outside, but inside it ionises a lot, right next to the body's cells.

wrong.other: Not quite: alpha ionises a lot, and inside the body nothing shields you.
wrong.far: Not quite: alpha only travels a few cm in air and is easily stopped. It is dangerous inside because it ionises so much right next to the body's cells.
wrong.unstoppable: Not quite: paper or skin stops alpha. Inside the body, though, there is no skin in the way, and it ionises a lot.

idk.hint: Outside, the skin stops alpha. What changes once the source is inside you?

steps.answerWhy: Alpha is highly ionising. Outside, the skin stops it; inside, nothing is in the way, so it does a lot of damage.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is an alpha particle, and what stops it?
points: stopped by paper (or skin, or a few cm of air)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: an alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons, like a helium nucleus, and a sheet of paper stops it.

steps.text: The second kind of radiation is beta (β). A beta particle is a fast-moving electron given out by the nucleus.
Where does an electron in the nucleus come from? A neutron turns into a proton and an electron. The new electron shoots out as the beta particle; the proton stays behind.
In beta decay, then, the nucleus gains one proton: its atomic number goes up by 1. A proton has the same relative mass as a neutron, so the mass number stays the same.

steps.question: Carbon-14 has atomic number 6. It gives out a beta particle. What is the atomic number of the new nucleus?
steps.right: Yes: 7. A neutron became a proton, so 6 + 1 = 7. Atomic number 7 is nitrogen.

wrong.other: Not quite: 7. The atomic number goes up by 1.
wrong.down: Not quite: in beta decay a neutron turns into a proton, so the nucleus gains a proton: 6 + 1 = 7.
wrong.same: Not quite: the mass number stays the same, but the atomic number goes up by 1, because a neutron became a proton: 7.

idk.hint: In beta decay, a neutron turns into a proton. Does the number of protons go up or down?

steps.answerWhy: A neutron turns into a proton, so the atomic number goes up by 1: 6 + 1 = 7.

steps.text: Beta is moderately ionising: less than alpha, more than gamma. So it travels further than alpha: about 1 m in air. A sheet of aluminium a few millimetres thick stops it.

steps.question: Which of these stops beta radiation?
steps.right: Yes: a few millimetres of aluminium stop beta.

wrong.other: Not quite: aluminium a few mm thick.
wrong.paper: Not quite: paper stops alpha, not beta. Beta gets through paper but is stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
wrong.nothing: Not quite: that is gamma. Beta is stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

idk.hint: Paper stops alpha. Beta gets further than alpha. Which material is the stronger barrier?

steps.answerWhy: Beta passes through paper but is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is a beta particle, and what stops it?
points: a fast-moving electron from the nucleus
stopped by a few mm of aluminium
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: a beta particle is a fast electron from the nucleus, and a few millimetres of aluminium stop it.

steps.text: The third kind is gamma. Gamma rays (γ) are not particles but waves of energy, like light, with far more energy.
Waves of energy that travel like light are called electromagnetic radiation. Radio waves and X-rays are other kinds. Gamma rays come from a nucleus.
Gamma has no mass and no charge. So when a nucleus gives out gamma, its mass number and atomic number stay the same. Gamma often comes out just after an alpha or beta decay.
Gamma is weakly ionising: it makes few ions, so it travels a long way through air and through the body. Thick lead or thick concrete reduces it a lot, but never stops it completely.
The picture puts all three side by side: alpha ends at the paper, beta ends at the aluminium, and some gamma still gets through the lead.

steps.question: A detector picks up radiation that gets through a few millimetres of aluminium. Which kind is it?
steps.right: Yes: only gamma gets through aluminium.

wrong.beta: Not quite: a few mm of aluminium stops beta. Only gamma gets through.
wrong.alpha: Not quite: paper stops alpha, so it could never get through aluminium. Only gamma does.

idk.hint: Paper stops alpha, and a few mm of aluminium stop beta. Which kind is left?

steps.answerWhy: Aluminium stops alpha and beta, so radiation that gets through it is gamma.

steps.text: To choose radiation for a job, compare how far each kind penetrates, its range in air and how strongly it ionises.
For example, to detect a source from outside the body, use gamma: it passes out through the body to a detector. Alpha and beta would be absorbed inside the body.

steps.question: Which radiation is the most strongly ionising?
steps.right: Yes: alpha is the most ionising, then beta, then gamma.

wrong.gamma: Not quite: gamma is the least ionising, which is why it travels so far. Alpha is the most ionising.
wrong.beta: Not quite: beta is in the middle. Alpha is the most ionising, which is why it is stopped so easily.

idk.hint: The one that is stopped most easily uses up its energy fastest, making ions. Which is stopped by paper?

steps.answerWhy: Alpha is the most ionising, then beta, then gamma.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is gamma radiation, and what does lead do to it?
points: electromagnetic radiation (waves, no mass or charge)
thick lead reduces it but does not stop it completely
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: gamma is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus, and thick lead reduces it but never stops it completely.

steps.text: Radiation is not only made by people. Background radiation is low-level radiation that is around us all the time, from natural and man-made sources.
The biggest natural source in the UK is radon, a radioactive gas that seeps out of some rocks. Another is cosmic rays, radiation from space. Rocks, buildings, food and drink add a little.
Man-made means made by people on purpose or by accident. Man-made sources include medical X-rays, fallout from nuclear weapons tests, and nuclear accidents.
Fallout is radioactive dust that spreads through the air after a nuclear explosion or accident, then slowly settles.

steps.question: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?
steps.right: Yes: radon comes out of rocks, so it is natural.

wrong.other: Not quite: radon gas from rocks.
wrong.xray: Not quite: X-rays are made by machines in hospitals, so they are man-made. Radon gas comes from rocks: natural.
wrong.accident: Not quite: an accident at a nuclear power station is man-made. Radon gas comes from rocks: natural.

idk.hint: Which of these would exist even if people had never built anything?

steps.answerWhy: Radon gas from rocks is natural; X-rays and nuclear accidents are man-made.

steps.text: How much radiation a person receives is their dose, measured in sieverts (Sv). 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 Sv.
Your background dose depends on where you live, since some rocks give out more radon. It also depends on your job: working with X-rays adds to it.
Now the numbers in decay. A decay written with symbols is called a nuclear equation. The mass numbers must add up to the same on both sides, and so must the atomic numbers.
An alpha particle is written ⁴₂He. Radium-226 gives out alpha and becomes radon-222: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. Top numbers: 226 = 222 + 4. Bottom: 88 = 86 + 2.
A beta particle is written ⁰₋₁e: mass number 0, and −1 at the bottom for its charge. Carbon-14 becomes nitrogen-14: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e. Bottom: 6 = 7 + (−1).
To find the new nucleus: write the starting nucleus, write the radiation with its numbers, then work out the numbers left over.

steps.question: Radon-222, ²²²₈₆Rn, gives out an alpha particle. What is the atomic number of the new nucleus?
steps.right: Yes: 84. The alpha particle takes 2 protons: 86 − 2 = 84.

wrong.add: Not quite: 84. The nucleus loses the alpha particle, so take 2 away: 86 − 2 = 84.
wrong.four: Not quite: 84. Take 2 off the atomic number (the 2 protons) and 4 off the mass number: 86 − 2 = 84.
wrong.mass: Not quite: 84. 218 is the new mass number, 222 − 4. The atomic number is 86 − 2 = 84.

idk.hint: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He. Take its bottom number away from 86.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle has atomic number 2, so the new atomic number is 86 − 2 = 84.

steps.prompt: In one line: what must be true of the numbers in a nuclear equation?
points: the mass numbers (top) add up the same on both sides
the atomic numbers (bottom) add up the same on both sides
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the mass numbers on each side add up to the same total, and so do the atomic numbers.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: what is an alpha particle made of?

options.text: A helium atom with its electrons

steps.right: Yes: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, a helium nucleus.

wrong.w1: Not quite: that is a beta particle. An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it has no electrons: it is a helium nucleus, 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

steps.answerWhy: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons: a helium nucleus.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?

wrong.w1: Not quite: beta needs a few mm of aluminium. Paper stops alpha.
wrong.w2: Not quite: gamma is only reduced, by thick lead. Paper stops alpha.

steps.answerWhy: Alpha is stopped by a sheet of paper.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: in beta decay, what happens to the mass number?
steps.right: Yes: it stays the same; the atomic number goes up by 1.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays the same.
wrong.w1: Not quite: that is alpha decay. In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton, so the mass number stays the same.
wrong.w2: Not quite: the atomic number goes up by 1. The mass number stays the same.

steps.answerWhy: A neutron turns into a proton, so the mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: which is a man-made source of background radiation?
steps.right: Yes: X-rays are made by machines.

wrong.w1: Not quite: cosmic rays come from space: natural. Medical X-rays are man-made.
wrong.w2: Not quite: radon comes from rocks: natural. Medical X-rays are man-made.

steps.answerWhy: Medical X-rays are man-made; cosmic rays and radon are natural.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: a source has an activity of 50 Bq. How many of its nuclei decay in 10 seconds?
steps.right: Yes: 50 each second for 10 seconds is 500.

wrong.other: Not quite: 500. 50 decays each second × 10 s = 500.

steps.answerWhy: 50 Bq is 50 decays each second, so in 10 s: 50 × 10 = 500.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: what is the unit of radiation dose?
steps.right: Yes: dose is measured in sieverts.

wrong.w1: Not quite: the becquerel is the unit of activity. Dose is in sieverts.
wrong.w2: Not quite: that is a count rate. Dose is in sieverts.

steps.answerWhy: Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv); activity is in becquerels (Bq).

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
